Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Solara Renewables Q3 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. Participants may press star then one on their touchtone phone if they would like to register for the Q&A session. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Solara Renewables's results for the Q3. Joining me on today's call are Elena Vasquez, Chief Executive Officer; Marcus Hale, Chief Financial Officer; Jordan Lee, Chief Development Officer; Dr. Nina Patel, Chief Technology Officer; Liam Chen, Chief Sustainability Officer; and Sarah Novak, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call will contain forward-looking statements. We encourage you to review the disclaimer in our press release and on our website regarding these statements.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Elena Vasquez.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Solara Renewables delivered exceptional results in the Q3, showcasing our leadership in the renewable energy sector. Our success is attributable to our innovative technologies, strategic partnerships, and unwavering commitment to sustainability.

Today, I want to highlight seven key aspects of our performance. First, the significant new PPAs we've secured along with favorable average PPA pricing. Second, our robust revenue and earnings growth. Third, our updated capacity addition guidance and impressive pipeline targets. Fourth, progress in tax equity financing and project-level financing. Fifth, the major market trends influencing our trajectory and their positive impact. Sixth, our prudent management of debt levels and financing costs. And seventh, ongoing PPA pricing trends and successful contract extensions.

These achievements position us strongly for the future. Now, I'll hand over the call to Marcus Hale to provide a detailed review of our financial results.

Marcus Hale:
Thank you, Elena. Our financial performance in the Q3 was outstanding. Revenue reached $452 million, representing a 35% increase compared to the same period last year. This growth was driven by significant project commissioning and increased energy production. Our gross margin expanded to 28.2%, reflecting improved operational efficiency and cost management. Operating expenses totaled $44 million, primarily due to investments in R&D and sales and marketing. Net income was $65 million, or $0.72 per share. We ended the quarter with $1.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are raising our full-year guidance for revenue and earnings.

Good morning, everyone. I'll now dive into our Q3 fiscal 2024 results, with a particular focus on revenue and earnings growth, which underscore the accelerating momentum in our core solar PV, offshore wind, and energy storage businesses. As a reminder, we're reporting on a GAAP basis unless otherwise noted, and all comparisons are year-over-year unless specified.

Starting with the headline numbers: Q3 revenue came in at $452 million, representing a robust 35% increase from $335 million in Q3 2023. This brings our fiscal year-to-date revenue to $1.28 billion, up 42% from $902 million in the prior-year period. Trailing twelve-month revenue now stands at $1.72 billion, positioning us for our first $2 billion full-year revenue run-rate as we capitalize on the global clean energy buildout.

Let me break this down by segment to highlight the drivers. Our Solar Solutions segment, which includes utility-scale modules, bifacial panels, and tracker systems, delivered $285 million in Q3 revenue—60% of total—up 48% YoY. This was fueled by record shipments of 1.8 GWdc from our new Arizona TOPCon cell gigafactory, which ramped to 80% utilization ahead of schedule. Key wins included a 500 MWdc PPA with Southern California Edison and progress on our 1.2 GW portfolio in the Southwest, where falling module costs—now at $0.28 per watt domestically—combined with IRA Section 45X manufacturing credits averaging $0.12 per watt, delivered exceptional economics.

Wind Energy, at 22% of revenue or $100 million, grew 25% YoY, driven by turbine deliveries for the 400 MW Vineyard Wind 1 project off Massachusetts, where we're supplying 10 MW Siemens Gamesa-style offshore turbines with integrated recyclability features to meet Jones Act compliance. Despite some permitting headwinds in the U.S. Northeast, our European backlog—bolstered by REPowerEU funding—grew 15% sequentially to €2.1 billion equivalent.

Energy Storage Systems hit $55 million, or 12% of mix, surging 65% YoY on the back of our LFP battery packs for C&I applications. We deployed 250 MWh in Q3, including a landmark 100 MWh four-hour system for a Texas data center client partnering with Equinix, leveraging our vertical integration from cathode production to BESS integration. Services and O&M rounded out at 6%, up modestly on long-term contracts.

Geographically, North America accounted for 58% of Q3 revenue, up from 52% last year, thanks to IRA-driven domestic content bonuses—we now qualify for 100% adder on nearly all U.S. projects. EMEA contributed 28%, with strong uptake in Spain's PERTE auctions and Germany's EEG revisions favoring hybrid solar-wind-storage. APAC was 14%, tempered by U.S. tariffs but offset by our Vietnam module assembly JV, which exported 600 MW to Australia under the Capacity Investment Scheme.

Turning to profitability: Gross margins expanded 420 basis points to 28.2% in Q3 from 24% prior year, our highest in five quarters. This reflects a favorable product mix—heavy on high-margin trackers and storage—scale efficiencies from our 5 GW annual cell capacity, and pass-through of raw material cost declines; polysilicon spot prices fell another 8% QoQ to $7.5/kg. Adjusted EBITDA reached $92 million, or 20.4% margin, up from $58 million or 17.3% last year—a 58% growth rate. Non-GAAP net income was $65 million, or $0.72 diluted EPS, beating our guidance midpoint by 10%.

OpEx as a percentage of revenue declined to 9.8% from 11.2%, driven by disciplined R&D spend at $28 million (6% of revenue), focused on next-gen perovskite-silicon tandem cells targeting 32% efficiency by 2026—lab results hit 30.5% this quarter—and our Naion solid-state battery pilot, which promises 50% higher energy density than LFP at comparable costs.

Strategically, these results validate our "Hub-and-Spoke" model: centralized U.S. manufacturing hubs feeding regional spokes for rapid deployment, de-risking supply chains amid Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act scrutiny. We've gained 150 bps market share in U.S. utility-scale solar to 12%, per Wood Mackenzie, outpacing peers like First Solar on cost while matching Enphase on tracker reliability. Our $4.5 billion backlog—up 30% YoY—provides 2.5x visibility, with 70% back-loaded into FY25-26 on fixed-price EPC contracts at blended LCOE under $25/MWh.

Looking ahead, we see sustained tailwinds from U.S. BLMs approving 5 GW of new solar leases in the West, EU's Net-Zero Industry Act fast-tracking permits, and China's oversupply normalizing as domestic demand absorbs 100 GW annually. Risks remain around interest rates pressuring PPAs and offshore wind cable delays, as seen with Ørsted's U.S. projects, but our 85% fixed-price backlog and $1.2 billion liquidity shield us.

For Q4, we guide revenue to $480-510 million (32-40% YoY growth), adjusted EBITDA $105-115 million (22-23% margin), and full FY24 revenue $1.95-2.05 billion. This implies 45% top-line growth and 60% EPS expansion for the year.

I'm also pleased to dive into one of our key growth drivers: our Power Purchase Agreement pipeline and pricing dynamics. As you know, in the Clean Tech space, PPAs are the lifeblood of our contracted backlog, providing visibility into long-term revenue streams while de-risking development in an era of volatile merchant markets.

First, on new PPAs secured: In Q3 alone, we announced and executed 1.45 GW of new PPAs, bringing our total contracted backlog to 8.2 GW across 24 projects. This represents a 28% quarter-over-quarter increase and positions us to deliver over $4.2 billion in lifetime revenue at current pricing, assuming standard 20-25 year terms with typical escalators tied to CPI averaging 2.5%.

Breaking it down regionally and by counterparty—key for diversification:

U.S. Southwest (CAISO and WECC markets): 850 MW across three utility-scale solar-plus-storage projects. A flagship 450 MW deal with Southern California Edison locks in dispatchable power from our Gemini Valley project, featuring 700 MWdc of LONGi Hi-MO 7 bifacial modules on Nextracker single-axis trackers, paired with 200 MWh of Tesla Megapack 2XL storage for 4-hour firming. This PPA includes premiums for Resource Adequacy (RA) capacity and LCFS credits, reflecting California's aggressive 100% clean energy mandate by 2045.

ERCOT, Texas: 400 MW with a hyperscaler—Meta Platforms—for our Pecos Solar Farm expansion. This corporate PPA emphasizes 24/7 carbon-free matching, enabled by our integrated 150 MW/600 MWh BESS utilizing Fluence Cube platforms with AI-optimized bidding into ERCOT's ancillary services market. Texas remains a hotspot due to its deregulated grid and data center boom, where we've seen PPA uptake accelerate 35% YoY amid ERCOT's record renewables curtailment challenges.

PJM Interconnection (Northeast U.S.): 200 MW hybrid wind-solar PPA with a Fortune 100 industrial off-taker, PSEG. This leverages our 182 MW Virginia Plains onshore turbines from Vestas' V236-15.0 MW platform, co-located with 50 MWdc agrivoltaic solar using Trina Vertex N-type TOPCon modules. PJM's capacity auctions are tightening, with prices up 15% to $250/kW-year, driving hybrid PPAs like this for baseload-like profiles.

Strategically, these wins stem from our 'Tech-Forward Development' initiative, launched post-IRA. We've deployed proprietary AlenaYield optimization software—integrated with PVsyst and P90 energy yield models—to boost project IRRs to 12-14% at current rates, even with WACC up to 6.8%. By stacking ITC/HITC at 50-70% via domestic content (95% U.S.-sourced modules and racking), transferability, and adder bonuses for energy communities, we've compressed LCOE to $22-26/MWh P50 across the portfolio.

Now, turning to average PPA pricing: Our blended fleet average stands at $38.50/MWh (real, levelized), a modest 4.2% increase from $36.95/MWh in Q2 and up 8% YoY. This bucks the historical downtrend—PPA prices fell 15% from 2021 peaks of $45/MWh due to oversupply and capex deflation—but reflects macro tailwinds:

Interest rate sensitivity: With 10-year Treasuries at 4.2%, financing costs rose 20 bps QoQ, flowing through to pricing via our dynamic term sheet models. We've hedged 70% of debt exposure using green bonds at SOFR+150 bps.

Inflation and supply chain: Module prices stabilized at $0.28/Wdc (down from $0.45 peak), but tracker and BOS costs ticked up 5% on steel tariffs. Still, N-type efficiencies >23% keep CAPEX flat YoY at $0.92/Wdc.

Green premiums: 25% of new volume carries $5-8/MWh uplifts for PPAs with REC bundling (e.g., Tier 1 Gold for EU CBAM compliance) and shapeability. Corporate buyers like Meta are paying 10-15% above utility LCOE for Scope 2 decarbonization.

Trend-wise, we're seeing bifurcation: Utility PPAs averaging $35/MWh in sunny ISOs, versus $45/MWh hybrids in capacity-constrained queues like MISO/SPP. Our forward curve projects stabilization at $37-40/MWh through 2025, supported by EIA's AEO2024 forecast of 25 GW annual solar additions.

Looking ahead, our 5 GW development pipeline—60% shovel-ready—targets 2.5 GW of new PPAs in FY24, with a focus on 'firm renewables' via 8-hour storage and green hydrogen offtake pilots (e.g., our 50 MW electrolyzer tie-in with Plug Power). This positions Solara to capture 15% market share in U.S. corporate PPAs, outpacing peers like NextEra and Clearway amid the hyperscaler rush for 50 GW+ by 2030.

As we pivot to forward-looking guidance, I'd like to provide a comprehensive update on our capacity addition outlook and project pipeline. This remains a cornerstone of our growth strategy in the renewable energy sector, where we're leveraging falling levelized cost of energy—or LCOE—for solar and wind, now down to $25-30/MWh unsubsidized in key markets like ERCOT and CAISO, alongside the tailwinds from the Inflation Reduction Act's ITC and PTC extensions, including the critical 45X domestic content and manufacturing credits.

First, a quick look back: In FY2023, we successfully commissioned 2.8 GWdc of capacity across our portfolio—60% utility-scale solar PV, 25% onshore wind, and 15% battery energy storage systems, or BESS—achieving 105% of our original guidance. This included flagship projects like the 500 MWdc SunForge solar farm in Texas, which hit commercial operation date, or COD, ahead of schedule in Q4, and our 300 MW / 600 MWh BESS hybrid in California, co-located with existing solar to optimize curtailment and capture ancillary services revenue under CAISO's resource adequacy mandates.

Turning to FY2024 guidance: We're raising our capacity addition target to 3.2-3.6 GWdc, up from our prior 2.8-3.2 GW range. This reflects stronger-than-expected PPA offtake, with 85% of new additions already contracted at blended PPAs of $35/MWh fixed over 15-20 years, and accelerating supply chain efficiencies. Breakdown by technology:

Solar PV: 2.0-2.3 GWdc (62% of total), driven by our next-gen bifacial TOPCon modules sourced via long-term offtake with First Solar and our own Arizona thin-film fab, qualifying for full 45X credits. Average module costs have compressed 18% YoY to $0.22/Wdc, enabling IRRs north of 12% post-tax.

Onshore Wind: 0.7-0.9 GWac (22%), with 15.X MW Siemens Gamesa turbines deployed in our Midwest portfolio, targeting high-capacity factor sites >45% in MISO and SPP. We've derisked permitting via early FERC queue positioning.

BESS and Hybrids: 0.5-0.6 GW / 1.2 GWh (16%), emphasizing 4-hour lithium-iron-phosphate systems from CATL partnerships, with pilots for 8-hour flow batteries using Form Energy tech to address duck curve challenges.

Regionally, 65% of FY2024 additions are U.S.-focused—primarily Texas (ERCOT) and California (CAISO), where interconnection queues have shortened post-FERC Order 2023 reforms, now averaging 18-24 months to energized. Europe contributes 20%, led by a 400 MW portfolio in the UK’s RO-CFD auctions and Germany’s EEG auctions, benefiting from €100 billion REPowerEU funding. The remaining 15% is APAC, with 250 MW in India’s SECI auctions and Australia’s VRET tenders, where we've secured hybrid wind-solar-BESS PPAs at AUD 55/MWh.

For FY2025, we're guiding to 4.2-4.8 GWdc, a 30%+ increase, contingent on continued capex discipline at $1.1-1.2 million/MW blended. This assumes 90% FID achievement on shovel-ready projects by year-end and no material supply disruptions from polysilicon volatility, which we've hedged via forward contracts.

Now, on our industry-leading pipeline: As of Q3 end, our total project pipeline stands at 52 GWdc—up 15% QoQ and 40% YoY—comprising 15 GW advanced-stage (permitting complete, PPAs in negotiation or executed), 22 GW mid-stage (early development, land secured), and 15 GW early-stage (greenfield origination). This positions us in the top quintile among peers like NextEra and Ørsted, with a 3-4x conversion ratio to backlog over 3 years.

Key pipeline highlights:

U.S. (55% of pipeline, 28.6 GW): 8 GW advanced, including the 1.2 GW Liberty Wind-Solar-BESS cluster in PJM, leveraging our 80% domestic content for IRA stacking (base ITC + 10% adder). We're targeting 20 GW CODs by 2027, with 70% contracted via corporates like Google and Amazon under VPPA structures.

Europe (25%, 13 GW): 4 GW advanced offshore wind, partnering with Vestas on 16 MW+ platforms for Dutch and Scottish North Sea farms. Trends here include hybrid offshore models with green hydrogen electrolyzers, where we're piloting 100 MW H2 output tied to a 1 GW wind array, aligning with EU's Net-Zero Industry Act.

Emerging Markets (20%, 10.4 GW): India and Brazil lead with 5 GW solar-wind hybrids, capitalizing on USD 1.5/W falling BoS costs. In Australia, our 2 GW portfolio eyes Snowy 2.0 grid upgrades.

Strategically, we're prioritizing three initiatives to accelerate conversion:

1. Tech Innovation: Rolling out tracker-less agrivoltaics on 30% of new solar (boosting yields 15-20% via sheep grazing), and long-duration storage (LDES) pilots exceeding 100 hours, positioning for DOE grants.

2. M&A and Partnerships: $2-3 billion dry powder for bolt-ons, like our recent $500 million acquisition of a 3 GW East Coast developer, echoing Enel's playbook. JV with Brookfield for 5 GW U.S. BESS manufacturing.

3. Risk Mitigation: 95% supply chain localization (U.S./EU), inflation-linked EPC contracts, and AI-driven yield optimization via our proprietary VerdantOS platform, which has lifted portfolio P50 energies 5% above nameplate.

In summary, our capacity guidance and pipeline underscore Solara Renewables's path to 15 GW cumulative additions by 2027, delivering FCF yields >10% and ROIC expansion to 11-13%. We're well-insulated against headwinds like interest rate persistence via fixed-debt refinancings at SOFR+150bps, and macro tailwinds from global decarbonization mandates.

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our capital structure, with a particular focus on tax equity financing and project-level financing. These mechanisms remain the bedrock of our growth strategy in the renewable energy sector, enabling us to scale our 2.3 GW operational portfolio and advance our 52 GW development pipeline across solar PV, onshore wind, and hybrid solar-plus-storage projects. In Q3 alone, we achieved financial close on over $1.8 billion in combined tax equity and project debt commitments, supporting 1.1 GW of near-term CODs targeted for 2025-2026.

Let me start with tax equity financing, which continues to be our primary avenue for monetizing the lucrative tax attributes generated by our projects under the Inflation Reduction Act—or IRA, as we all know it. For context, tax equity investors—predominantly large U.S. banks like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and insurance giants such as MetLife and Prudential—provide upfront capital in exchange for a share of the project's ITC, PTC, and Section 45X/48E credits, along with a portion of cash flows until their targeted IRR hurdles are met. This structure is especially critical for utility-scale assets, where base ITC yields can hit 30% for standalone solar, jumping to 50-70% with adders for domestic content, energy communities, and low-income housing under LCIA provisions.

In Q3, we closed a landmark $850 million tax equity facility with a consortium led by Wells Fargo and US Bancorp for our 650 MW SunForge portfolio in ERCOT and MISO South. This included a classic 'fixed-flip' structure: investors take 99% of tax benefits and cash flows until they achieve a 7.5% unlevered IRR and full ITC/PTC recapture, flipping to a 20/80 split thereafter favoring our sponsor equity. Pricing was attractive at an HAIT multiple of 1.85x—up from 1.65x last year—reflecting compressed yields amid higher interest rates but bolstered by IRA transferability. Speaking of which, we've transferred $220 million in standalone credits this quarter at 92-95% of face value through platforms like Crux and Arcadia, reducing our historical reliance on tax equity by 25% for greenfield projects. This hybrid approach has lowered our all-in cost of capital to 5.2% on tax-advantaged assets, versus 6.8% for merchant exposure.

Regionally, U.S. tax equity remains robust, with $25-30 billion in annual capacity per recent Lazard reports, though we're seeing tightening in CAISO due to interconnection delays pushing out 300 MW of our queue. In contrast, Europe—where we're ramping via our 400 MW offshore wind JV with Ørsted in the UK—relies less on tax equity, favoring P72 PPAs and EPCI financing. There, green bonds from the EIB have supplemented our deals at sub-3% yields.

Shifting to project-level financing, this non-recourse debt layered atop tax equity and our 20-25% sponsor equity slice provides the high leverage needed for ROIC in the mid-teens. We're targeting 55-65% debt ratios on construction financings, transitioning to 75-80% on term debt post-COD, with DSCRs held at 1.45x minimum. In Q3, we secured $950 million in project debt across four assets: a $400 million green loan from MUFG and DNB for our 300 MW WindHaven project in PJM, fixed at SOFR + 145 bps (effective 4.75% all-in after swaps), and a $550 million construction facility from Santander and ING for our 450 MW SolStor hybrid in Arizona's APS territory—featuring 200 MWh of 4-hour BESS with Tesla Megapacks for FIRM capacity dispatch.

Key trends here include the surge in back-leverage facilities: we drew $180 million against our stabilized portfolio at 5.25% fixed via a $1.2 billion revolver upsized with Citi, funding bolt-on storage retrofits on legacy assets. Interest rate hedging is table stakes—95% of our drawdowns are swapped out to 2028 at an average 4.2%—mitigating the 150 bps Fed hike impact since 2022. Storage integration is a game-changer: our hybrids now command 20-30% FOM uplift in IRRs, with tax equity HAITs exceeding 2.0x thanks to ITC bonus depreciation on BESS.

Strategically, we're optimizing via 'master forward' LCIA commitments with the Treasury, locking in 45V/45Z credits for our 500 MW electrolyzer pipeline in Texas, and partnering with Nextracker for 80% U.S.-content bifacial systems to max domestic adders. This positions us ahead of peers like NextEra and Invenergy, who report similar flips but lag on transferability scale. Risks? Supply chain inflation on trackers (up 8% YoY per SEIA data) and policy uncertainty post-election, but our 70% hedged pipeline and $2.5 billion liquidity buffer insulate us.

Overall, these financings underscore our disciplined approach: $4.2 billion closed YTD against a $12 billion five-year target, with implied GW-scale economics at $1.1 million/MW all-in capex. We're not just building projects; we're architecting capital stacks for sustained 15-18% levered IRRs in a decarbonizing grid.

Before I dive into the quarter's financials more deeply, I'd like to spend a few minutes on the significant market trends shaping our industry and their direct impact on Solara Renewables. As a leader in utility-scale solar PV, bifacial module manufacturing, and integrated energy storage solutions, we're positioned at the epicenter of the clean tech revolution. Let me break this down into key trends, supported by data from sources like the IEA's Renewables 2024 report, BloombergNEF, and our own proprietary modeling.

Trend 1: Accelerated Solar PV Deployment Amid Plunging LCOE.

The most dominant trend remains the explosive growth in solar photovoltaic installations, driven by module cost declines and improving capacity factors. Globally, solar added a record 447 GWdc in 2023—up 87% year-over-year—surpassing wind for the first time, and we're on track for over 500 GWdc in 2024 per BNEF forecasts. This is fueled by a 42% drop in average module prices to around $0.22 per watt in Q3 2024, thanks to overcapacity in China, where Tier 1 manufacturers like LONGi and JinkoSolar flooded the market with TOPCon and nascent HJT (heterojunction) cells.

For Solara Renewables, this translates to outsized opportunities. Our domestic U.S. module production—now at 8 GW annual nameplate capacity in our Arizona and Texas fabs—has shielded us from AD/CVD tariffs, allowing us to capture 15% market share in IRA-eligible projects. We've seen our average selling price hold steady at $0.38/W, versus the global spot price, yielding a robust 25% gross margin on modules. Impact: This trend boosted our Q3 solar EPC revenue by 62% YoY to $1.2 billion, with a $12.4 billion backlog extending visibility through 2027. Strategically, we're investing $450 million in next-gen perovskite-silicon tandem cells, targeting a 28%+ efficiency jump by 2026, which could slash our project LCOE below $25/MWh in sunny markets like the U.S. Southwest.

Trend 2: Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) Boom and Hybridization.

Energy storage is the hottest growth vector, with global deployments hitting 75 GW/170 GWh in 2023—a 50% YoY surge—and projections for 140 GW/400 GWh in 2024. Dispatchable renewables are king: hybrid solar-plus-storage projects now represent 65% of U.S. interconnection queues, per Wood Mackenzie data. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) packs dominate at 60% cost reductions since 2020, but supply chain bottlenecks in cathode precursors and BMS (battery management systems) have pushed system prices to $140/kWh.

At Solara Renewables, our integrated SolaraFlow BESS—featuring our proprietary vanadium redox flow tech alongside LFP—has been a game-changer. We've deployed 2.5 GW/10 GWh YTD, up 120% YoY, with four-hour duration projects commanding premiums in CAISO and ERCOT markets. Margins here are stellar at 32% EBITDA, thanks to our 1.2 GWh flow battery pilot scaling to commercial. Impact: Storage contributed $850 million to Q3 revenue, 28% of total, and de-risked our 52 GWdc solar pipeline by enabling 24/7 dispatchability. Regional note: In Europe, where TSOs like TenneT demand 100 MW/400 MWh standalone storage for grid stability, we've secured €1.2 billion in PPAs under the REPowerEU plan. Our insight: We're pivoting 30% of capex to long-duration storage (8+ hours) to capture the $50 billion U.S. LDES market by 2030, partnering with Form Energy on iron-air tech.

Trend 3: Policy Tailwinds and Corporate Demand Surge.

Government incentives are supercharging adoption. The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) has unlocked $110 billion in investment tax credits through 2032, with transferability enabling hyperscalers like Google and Amazon—responsible for 40% of new U.S. PPAs—to ink 25 GW of deals in 2024 alone. In Europe, the Net-Zero Industry Act aims for 50% domestic solar content by 2030, while China's 1,200 GW wind+solar target by 2030 sustains manufacturing dominance but sparks trade tensions.

Impacts on us are profoundly positive: IRA adders have lifted our effective ITC to 50-60% on domestic content projects, driving 45% YoY growth in our U.S. segment to $2.1 billion in Q3. Our 2.8 GW corporate PPA portfolio— including a landmark 1 GW deal with Microsoft for our Texas Panhandle hybrid farm—now yields fixed $45/MWh pricing, insulating us from merchant volatility. Challenges persist: Rising interest rates have compressed P50 IRRs from 9% to 7.5% on levered projects, but our $4.5 billion green bond issuance at 4.2% fixed keeps WACC low at 5.8%.

Regional Commentary and Strategic Insights:

U.S. (65% of revenue): IRA-driven boom in ERCOT and PJM; our 10 GW interconnection queue positions us for 20% CAGR through 2028. Insight: Accelerating vertical integration with Enphase IQ8 microinverters for trackerless agrivoltaics, targeting 15% yield uplift on dual-use farmland.

Europe (20%): Supply chain localization amid Ukraine fallout; €800 million in German and Spanish auctions won YTD. Headwind: Permitting delays averaging 18 months. Insight: €300 million JV with Ørsted for offshore floating solar, tapping 100 GW potential.

Asia-Pacific/LatAm (15%): China module glut pressures exports, but Brazil's 25 GW auction pipeline offers upside. Insight: Hedging 70% of polysilicon exposure via forward contracts at $8/kg.

Overall, these trends affirm our full-year guidance: $6.8-7.2 billion revenue (35% YoY growth), 28-30% adjusted EBITDA margins, and $1.1 billion free cash flow. We're raising our 2025 solar deployment outlook to 12 GWdc, factoring in 510 GW global additions. Risks include interconnection backlogs (now 2.5 years in CAISO) and potential IRA clawbacks, but our $18 billion backlog—up 40% YoY—provides a fortress balance sheet.

As we dive into our balance sheet strength, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our debt levels and financing costs—a critical area where we've continued to execute strategically amid a dynamic macroeconomic environment and the unique capital demands of our renewable energy portfolio. Our disciplined approach to capital structure has allowed us to fund over 2.5 GW of new solar, wind, and battery storage projects this year while maintaining robust liquidity and competitive financing costs.

Starting with the headline figures: As of September 30th, our total gross debt stood at $5.2 billion, up 8% year-over-year from $4.8 billion, primarily driven by construction financing for our 1.2 GW Atlantic Breeze offshore wind project off the U.S. East Coast and the 800 MW Desert Sun utility-scale solar-plus-storage facility in the Southwest. Net debt, after adjusting for $1.4 billion in unrestricted cash and equivalents, came in at $3.8 billion. This reflects a healthy net debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 3.4x—comfortably within our target range of 3.0x to 4.0x and improved from 3.7x at year-end 2023. For context, this compares favorably to peers like NextEra Energy, which reports around 3.8x, and Ørsted at 4.2x, underscoring our conservative leverage amid rising capex needs.

Breaking it down by tenor and type: 85% of our debt is long-term, with an average maturity of 7.2 years, minimizing refinancing risk in a higher-for-longer rate environment. Short-term debt and revolver draws represent just 15%, or $780 million, fully supported by our $2.5 billion syndicated revolving credit facility, which remains undrawn beyond that and available through 2028. Fixed-rate debt comprises 72% of the total, hedging us against the Fed's recent 50 bps cut in September, while the remaining 28% is variable-rate, LIBOR-plus linked but capped via interest rate swaps covering 90% of that exposure out to 2027.

On financing costs, our weighted average cost of debt improved to 4.2% from 4.8% last quarter and 5.1% a year ago—a 180 bps year-over-year reduction that directly boosted our adjusted EBITDA by $45 million in Q3. This was achieved through several targeted initiatives. First, in July, we successfully refinanced $900 million of maturing term loans with a new green bond issuance under our EMTN program: a 10-year senior unsecured green bond priced at a record-low 3.5% coupon, upsized from €750 million due to strong demand from ESG-focused investors like BlackRock and European pension funds. This aligns with EU Taxonomy and ICMA Green Bond Principles, qualifying for our offshore wind and BESS projects.

Second, we've leveraged the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) transferability provisions aggressively. In Q3 alone, we monetized $320 million in transferable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) from our California BESS deployments at a 95% advance rate, effectively providing non-dilutive, zero-cost financing equivalent to 30% of project capex. This has lowered our all-in cost of capital for U.S. solar and storage to under 3.5%, compared to 5-6% pre-IRA. We've also locked in Production Tax Credits (PTCs) for our Midwest wind farms via long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with utilities like Duke Energy, stabilizing cash flows and supporting our A- credit rating from S&P.

Regionally, our U.S. operations—now 65% of our 12 GW portfolio—continue to benefit from IRA tailwinds, with debt costs averaging 3.8% versus 4.7% in Europe, where higher sovereign yields and policy uncertainty around the REPowerEU plan have pushed costs up. In APAC, our 1 GW Australian pipeline is financed via Kangaroo Bonds at 4.1%, bolstered by the Safeguard Mechanism reforms, though we're monitoring grid queue delays similar to those plaguing U.S. PJM and ERCOT interconnects. Latin America remains opportunistic, with $200 million in project finance for Chilean solar at SOFR-plus-225 bps, hedged against currency volatility.

Strategically, we're prioritizing sustainability-linked financing to further compress costs. Our recent $500 million sustainability-linked loan from a consortium including BNP Paribas ties margins to KPIs like carbon abatement (target: 15 MtCO2e annually by 2027) and diversity metrics, with a 15 bps incentive achieved ahead of schedule. We've also prepped a $1.5 billion ATM equity shelf for opportunistic raises, but with $1.8 billion in liquidity and $3.2 billion in contracted backlog, we have no immediate need—our priority is bolt-on M&A in high-IRR storage, like potential tuck-ins akin to Enphase's microinverter expansions.

Looking forward, we expect debt levels to peak at $5.8 billion by mid-2025 as we commission 3 GW of backlog, then delever to 3.0x net debt/EBITDA by 2026 through $1.2 billion in annual FCF generation at $60-70/MWh PPA pricing. Financing costs should trend toward 3.8-4.0% as we roll out more green hybrid securities and benefit from anticipated rate normalization. This positions us exceptionally well in a sector where capex intensity—$1.2-1.5 million per MW for offshore wind—demands flawless execution.

Before we open the line for Q&A, I'd like to dive deeper into one of our core value drivers: PPA pricing trends and contract extensions. As you know, Solara Renewables is a leading independent power producer with over 15 GW of operating renewables capacity across solar, wind, and hybrid storage assets, primarily in the US, Europe, and Australia. Our contracted backlog stands at 22 GW, with 85% fixed under long-term PPAs averaging 15 years remaining. Today, I'll unpack the dynamics shaping our PPA market, highlight recent wins, and share our strategic outlook.

Let's start with PPA pricing trends. The renewable PPA market has matured significantly since the post-IRA boom of 2022-2023, when merchant tailwinds and hyperscaler demand from the likes of Google, Amazon, and Microsoft drove aggressive bidding. However, we've seen a notable shift in 2024. Globally, average utility-scale solar PPA prices have stabilized at around $26-32 per MWh on a Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE)-adjusted basis, up 4-7% year-over-year from 2023 lows. Wind lags slightly at $28-38/MWh, reflecting higher turbine costs amid supply chain bottlenecks for components like rare-earth magnets.

In the US, our bread-and-butter market representing 65% of our pipeline, pricing has firmed considerably. ERCOT (Texas) PPAs averaged $29/MWh for solar-plus-storage hybrids in Q3 – a 12% premium over pure solar at $25/MWh – thanks to the 4-hour dispatchable profiles enabled by our Tesla Megapack integrations. This mirrors deals like NextEra's recent 800 MW Brazos Valley project at $30/MWh. In CAISO, where curtailment risks are higher, we've locked in $32/MWh for 500 MW of bifacial PERC-plus modules with 25% DC:AC ratios, benefiting from NEM 3.0's storage mandates. PJM and MISO, however, remain softer at $24-27/MWh due to interconnection queue backlogs – over 2,500 GW pending per FERC data – pushing developers toward repowers over greenfield.

Europe tells a bifurcated story. In the UK and Iberia, post-energy crisis inflation has boosted prices to €35-45/MWh ($38-49/MWh equivalent), with our 300 MW Spanish portfolio extension fetching €42/MWh including a 2% annual CPI escalator. Germany's EEG auctions, however, yielded €28/MWh for unsubsidized wind – down 8% YoY – amid negative pricing episodes in 2024's oversupplied grid. We're mitigating this via hybrid offtake with corporates like Unilever, who pay a 15-20% green premium for Scope 2 decarbonization.

Australia and emerging APAC markets are bright spots: AEMO-driven solar PPAs hit AUD 55/MWh ($36 USD), fueled by rooftop-to-utility scale convergence and battery undercutting peakers.

Key drivers behind this pricing resilience? First, cost inflation: Module prices rebounded 15% to $0.28/W for TOPCon tech, per IRENA Q3 data, while steel and EPC costs rose 10% on Red Sea disruptions. Second, higher interest rates: Our WACC climbed to 6.2% from 5.1% in 2023, necessitating $2-4/MWh uplifts to maintain 8-10% unlevered IRRs. Third, technical advancements: Capacity factors for our fixed-tilt solar hit 28% (vs. 24% industry avg), thanks to tracker optimizations and albedo-enhancing ground covers. Co-located BESS – now 40% of our US bids – commands $5-8/MWh firmness premiums, with round-trip efficiencies at 92% on our 200 MW/800 MWh Florida project.

On the buyer side, C&I and hyperscalers represent 45% of our Q3 signings, up from 30% last year. Their VPPA structures embed virtual delivery with fixed $/MWh strikes, hedging carbon credits under TCFD reporting. Utilities, facing FERC Order 2222 delays, are extending offtake for reliability – think Duke Energy's 1 GW RFP at $31/MWh.

Now, turning to contract extensions, this is where we generate outsized value from our 8 GW brownfield portfolio. With 40% of assets approaching year 15-20 terms, extensions preserve EBITDA margins at 75-80% while avoiding merchant exposure. In Q3, we executed 1.2 GW of extensions across 12 projects, adding $450 million to our 10-year backlog at an average blended price of $34/MWh – 25% above original strikes.

Take our 1 GW Midwest wind fleet: Repowered with Vestas V150-6.0 MW turbines (upgraded from 2 MW machines), we extended PPAs with MidAmerican Energy for 12 years at $36/MWh, incorporating 1.5% escalators and $2/MWh availability bonuses. Post-repower, capacity factors jumped from 35% to 42%, with LCOE dropping to $22/MWh despite $1.2 million/MW capex.

In California, we extended 400 MW solar with PG&E at $38/MWh, adding 100 MW/400 MWh Fluence Gridstack storage for curtailment arbitrage. This hybrid unlocked a 10-year term with revenue stacking from LCFS credits ($15/tonne CO2e) and capacity payments.

Europe extensions totaled 300 MW: UK offshore wind with Ørsted JV partners at £45/MWh, leveraging CfD auctions, and Italian solar repowers using HJT modules for 30% efficiency gains.

Strategically, our extension playbook emphasizes three pillars:

1. Repowering and hybridization: 70% of extensions include tech upgrades, targeting 15-20% EBITDA uplift. We've deployed AI-driven O&M via our proprietary GreenWave Analytics platform, reducing AEP downtime to 1.2% and boosting pricing power.

2. Inflation protections: All new extensions embed 1.5-2.5% CPI or PPA-linked escalators, shielding against the 3.2% US PPI energy inflation we've modeled.

3. Merchant tail management: For the 15% uncontracted exposure, we're layering short-term PPAs (3-5 years) and battery dispatch, achieving 95% capture rates in ERCOT's $100+/MWh summer spikes.

Looking forward, we guide 5-8% PPA pricing growth in 2025, driven by IRA Section 45X PTC adders ($27/MWh for wind through 2027) and EU CBAM tariffs pressuring importers. Risks include interconnection delays – we've derisked 90% of our 5 GW US queue – and policy shifts like potential US tax credit phaseouts post-2026. Mitigants: $2.5B undrawn revolver, 4.2x Net Debt/EBITDA, and 60% backlog inflation-hedged.

In summary, robust PPA trends and extensions underpin our raised FY24 EBITDA guidance to $1.8-1.9B (up 10% at midpoint) and 12-15% backlog growth to 25 GW. This positions Solara Renewables for 10%+ CAGR through the decade, capitalizing on the $1.7T global renewables investment need per BNEF.
